claims.text: A model combining disorder-sensitive data-driven descriptors with first-principles phonon calculations will predict low phonon thermal conductivity in high-entropy alloys more accurately than conventional approaches.
The target high-entropy alloys are disordered solid solutions with well-characterized phase stability and measured phonon thermal conductivity.
The predictive approach couples machine-learning algorithms with ab initio phonon-dispersion and phonon-scattering calculations.
Descriptors of chemical disorder and local bonding environments are incorporated into the predictive approach.
The approach is applicable to single-phase, disordered solid-solution high-entropy alloys with moderate variations in atomic radii and electronegativity.
Alloys containing secondary phases or extreme segregation may lie outside the model's reliable range.
Local chemical and structural disorder enhances phonon scattering.
Enhanced phonon scattering lowers thermal conductivity.
Variations in local atomic environments affect phonon lifetimes.
Variations in local atomic environments affect phonon group velocities.
Accounting for local-environment effects on phonon lifetimes and group velocities improves predictions of low thermal conductivity.
The integrated approach will reduce prediction error by at least 20% relative to conventional methods.
Conventional first-principles and heuristic methods do not fully account for multidimensional disorder effects in high-entropy alloys.
Significant microstructural or phase segregation introduces additional thermal-transport mechanisms that can limit the approach's accuracy.
Preliminary simulation trends support including disorder descriptors in the predictive model.
The magnitude of the prediction improvement remains uncertain until the approach is benchmarked against a diverse experimental dataset.
Failure to reduce prediction error by at least 20% relative to standard methods across the blind test set would falsify the hypothesis.
